stem: An elderly patient who has been diagnosed with COPD complains of persistent symptoms of shortness of breath despite smoking cessation and the use of a short acting bronchodilator. What would be the next line of therapy used to treat this patient?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

From 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease and 07 - Respiratory Pharmacology. COPD therapy is built on bronchodilation to reduce hyperinflation. The chart's treatment ladder runs from smoking cessation to LABA / LAMA (then dual bronchodilators), then ICS, then O2. If a patient is still breathless on an as-needed short-acting agent, the next step is a long-acting bronchodilator.

  • A (ICS): reserved for moderate–severe disease with persistent symptoms despite optimal bronchodilators, frequent exacerbations, or asthma-COPD overlap.
  • B (oxygen): for hypoxemia (target 88–92%), not for breathlessness alone.
  • C (LTRA): an asthma and allergic-rhinitis drug, not part of the COPD algorithm.
  • E (pulmonary rehab): the notes do not cover it. It is an adjunct and does not replace the missing maintenance bronchodilator.

stem: A patient who has been diagnosed with asthma demonstrates persistent symptoms of wheezing, nighttime cough and shortness of breath while exercising. Currently the patient is receiving a short acting β-agonist as the only mode of therapy. Her pulmonary function tests demonstrate persistent mild airflow obstruction. What would be the next appropriate therapeutic maneuver in this patient?

options.html: Maintain short acting β-agonist and start an inhaled corticosteroid
Stop short acting β-agonist and start a long acting β-agonist
Maintain short acting β-agonist and start a leukotriene receptor antagonist
Stop short acting β-agonist and start an inhaled corticosteroid
Maintain short acting β-agonist and start a long acting β-agonist and a leukotriene receptor antagonist

answer:
The correct answer is A.

From 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease and 07 - Respiratory Pharmacology. Inflammation is the root of airflow obstruction in asthma, so an inhaled corticosteroid is first-line controller therapy. The lecture says all patients, from mild to severe, should be on some form of ICS. She has night-time symptoms and persistent obstruction on a SABA alone, which is uncontrolled asthma by CTS criteria, so she needs an ICS added. The SABA stays as her reliever.

  • C: an LTRA is an add-on, a later step after ICS, not the first controller.
  • D: stopping the SABA removes her rescue inhaler for acute symptoms.

stem: Which of the following is true about chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)?

options.html: Smoking is the only known cause of COPD
The addition of long acting β-agonists to patients with severe airflow obstruction improves survival
Patients with mild disease will have lung function that normalizes when they are asymptomatic
The addition of inhaled corticosteroids to patients with moderate to severe COPD decreases the rate of exacerbations
Leukotriene receptor antagonists are used if patients remain symptomatic despite the use of a long-acting anticholinergic

answer:
The correct answer is D.

From 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease and 07 - Respiratory Pharmacology. ICS in COPD are indicated for moderate–severe disease with persistent symptoms, or for frequent exacerbations. The pharmacology lecture lists reducing the frequency and severity of exacerbations as a benefit of ICS. So D is true.

  • A: smoking causes over 90% of COPD but not all of it. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, pollution (indoor cooking) and immature lung development are also causes.
  • B: the lecture credits smoking cessation with improving survival. Bronchodilators reduce hyperinflation and symptoms, and no therapy repairs destroyed lung.
  • C: lung function does not normalize once COPD develops. Fixed obstruction, unlike asthma's variable obstruction, is what defines it.
  • E: LTRAs are asthma drugs. COPD escalates to triple therapy (LAMA + LABA + ICS).

stem: When comparing the pathophysiology of COPD and asthma, which of the following is true?

options.html: Both diseases are characterized by inflammation as the hallmark feature
Inhaled corticosteroids are considered as a first-line agent to treat symptoms in both diseases
Both diseases are characterized by variability in airflow obstruction
Dynamic hyperinflation can occur in both COPD and asthma
Alveolar destruction occurs in both COPD and asthma

answer:
The correct answer is D.

From 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease. Both diseases narrow the airway lumen, so both can trap gas: incomplete exhalation raises end-expiratory volume. The lecture singles this out as dynamic hyperinflation, worst when demand rises (exercise), in COPD and asthma alike.

  • A: inflammation is the root cause of obstruction in asthma. COPD's cardinal features are loss of alveolar attachments, mucosal inflammation/fibrosis and mucus hypersecretion.
  • B: ICS are first line for all asthma. In COPD they are added only for persistent symptoms despite bronchodilators, frequent exacerbations, or asthma–COPD overlap.
  • C: variable airflow obstruction defines asthma. COPD limitation is persistent.
  • E: alveolar wall destruction is emphysema (COPD), not asthma.

stem: A patient arrives at the ED with shortness of breath. Imaging reveals a hemothorax (blood accumulating in the pleural cavity). In which of the following recesses would fluid be most likely to accumulate when the patient is upright?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

From 02 - Anatomy of the Lungs and Thorax. The lecture names the costodiaphragmatic recess the deepest recess of the pleural cavity. It runs down beside the diaphragm to about the 8th–10th rib, and the lungs never fully fill it, even in inspiration. In an upright patient, fluid such as blood falls to the lowest point of the pleural cavity and pools there first. That is also why thoracentesis targets this recess.

  • B (costomediastinal recess): a small anterior space between the costal and mediastinal pleura that the lung edges fill during inspiration. It is neither dependent nor deep when upright.

stem: In the same patient with the hemothorax, where should you insert a needle, along the mid-axial line, to remove the fluid (thoracocentesis)?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

From 02 - Anatomy of the Lungs and Thorax. Fluid pools in the costodiaphragmatic recess, which reaches down to the 8th–10th rib and which the lung never fully fills. You want a site below the lung but above the diaphragm, so in the mid-axillary line (the stem's "mid-axial") that means a low interspace, the 9th. Expiration is the safer phase because the lung withdraws upward out of the recesses. In inspiration it expands down into them, bringing the lung into the needle's path.

  • A and B (5th space): too high. The needle would enter aerated lung rather than the dependent fluid, risking pneumothorax.
  • D: the right level, but at the wrong phase of breathing.

Pass the needle over the top of the rib, because the intercostal neurovascular bundle runs in the costal groove along the lower border.

stem: When performing a thoracocentesis (inserting a needle to remove the fluid), which of the following structures is of most concern and should be avoided when inserting the needle through the intercostal space into the costodiaphragmatic recess while the patient has exhaled?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

From 02 - Anatomy of the Lungs and Thorax. Every intercostal puncture must pass the intercostal neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve from superior to inferior). The bundle runs in the costal groove on the inferior border of each rib, between the internal and innermost intercostals. Keep the needle just above the upper border of the rib below.

  • A (diaphragm): rises on exhalation but sits below the recess floor. It is a hazard only if the needle is placed too low, not one met on every pass.
  • B (internal thoracic vessels): run parasternally on the anterior wall, away from a lateral/posterior tap.
  • D (intercostal muscles): must be traversed and are not what you avoid.
  • E (lungs): never fully occupy the costodiaphragmatic recess, and they withdraw further on exhalation.

stem: What is the normal pulmonary vascular response to low alveolar PO2 (PA02)?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

From 02 - Gas Exchange and Hypoxia. A low PAO2 triggers hypoxic arterial vasoconstriction. The pulmonary arterioles feeding poorly ventilated alveoli constrict, diverting blood to alveoli that can oxygenate it and restoring V/Q matching. 07 - Respiratory Pharmacology gives the same reflex in bronchospasm: vessels to underventilated regions constrict and vessels to well-ventilated regions dilate. The cost is that widespread or chronic hypoxia constricts the whole bed, which leads to pulmonary hypertension.

  • A: dilation is the systemic vascular response to hypoxia, the opposite of the lung's.
  • B and D: the response is arterial (pre-capillary), where flow is controlled, not venous.

stem:
Match the appropriate cause of hypoxemia to the clinical description:

  1. V/Q mismatch
  2. Shunt
  3. Hypoventilation
  4. Diffusion impairment

options.html: Large mucous plug completely occluding the left mainstem bronchus
Reduced minute ventilation due to narcotics
Interstitial fibrosis in a patient with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

answer:
A – ii; B – i; C – iii; D – iv.

From 02 - Gas Exchange and Hypoxia and the V/Q section of 03 - Lung Physiology - Ventilation. Map each lesion to what it does to ventilation, perfusion or the barrier:

  • A – shunt (ii): a plug completely occluding a mainstem bronchus leaves perfused lung with no ventilation (V/Q = 0). The lecture's partial mucous plugs only lower V/Q; total occlusion is a true shunt that 100% O2 will not correct.
  • B – V/Q mismatch (i): PE leaves lung ventilated but not perfused, i.e. dead space (V/Q → ∞).
  • C – hypoventilation (iii): narcotics suppress respiratory drive; PaCO2 rises and the A–a gradient stays normal.
  • D – diffusion impairment (iv): fibrosis thickens the blood–gas barrier (Fick's law), with ↓ DLCO.

preamble.title: Shared instructions
preamble.html:
Questions 21 and 22 relate to the following clinical scenario:

A patient is admitted with acute chest pain and cough following a flight home from India. In ED

the SP02 is 88% on room air. There is right calf swelling and tenderness. Chest X-ray is clear.

Arterial blood gas shows the following pH 7.47, Pa02 55 mmHg, Pac02 33 mmHg, HCO3 24

mmHg.

stem: What is the A-a gradient?
answer:
53 to 54.

From 02 - Gas Exchange and Hypoxia. Work through the alveolar gas equation on room air:

  • PIO2 = 0.21 × (760 − 47) = 150 mm Hg.
  • PAO2 = PIO2 − PaCO2/0.8 = 150 − 33/0.8 = 150 − 41 = about 108–109 mm Hg.
  • A–a gradient = PAO2 − PaO2 = 108.5 − 55 = about 53–54 mm Hg.

A normal gradient is age/4 + 4, roughly 10–20 in an adult, so this one is markedly raised. The hypoxemia therefore comes from the lung (shunt, V/Q mismatch or diffusion), not from hypoventilation or low inspired O2. The low PaCO2 reflects tachypnea. With a clear film after a long flight and a swollen calf, this is the pattern of pulmonary embolism (next question).

  • C (MI): chest pain fits, but not the DVT or the wide gradient on a clear film.
  • D (pneumonia): fills alveoli with exudate, so the CXR would show consolidation.

stem: A 57-year-old patient is ventilated for 2 weeks in the ICU following bypass surgery. He has COPD and has smoked 2 pks a day x 20 years. He develops fever, purulent sputum and consolidation on X ray. All of the following statements are true EXCEPT:

options.html: The patient probably acquired this infection in hospital.
Organisms causing nosocomial pneumonia are more sensitive to antibiotics than organisms causing community acquired pneumonia.
Gram negative bacilli are a common cause of nosocomial pneumonia.
Good hand washing and paying meticulous attention to keeping respiratory equipment clean may prevent nosocomial pneumonia.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

From 01 - Alveolar Causes of Dyspnea and 02 - Pneumonia. Fever, purulent sputum and new consolidation arising after 2 weeks of ventilation meet the lecture's definition of hospital-acquired disease: onset 48 h or more after admission or intubation, which here is VAP. The lecture separates nosocomial from community-acquired pneumonia by its Gram-negative organisms: aerobic GNRs such as E. coli and Klebsiella (60%), and Pseudomonas. That flora is more resistant, not less, which is why empiric therapy is broad anti-pseudomonal cover (piperacillin/tazobactam + vancomycin) rather than the CAP macrolide/ceftriaxone.

  • A, C: true, as above.
  • D: true. Hand hygiene and clean respiratory equipment block the transfer of hospital flora into ventilated airways. This is an infection-control principle rather than something the notes spell out.

stem: Concerning the diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide in a patient with diffuse interstitial lung disease, all of the following statements are true EXCEPT:

options.html: shows an abnormally small rise during exercise
is reduced partly because of the thickening of the blood gas barrier
is reduced partly because of the loss of pulmonary capillaries
is reduced only in very late stages of disease

answer:
The correct answer is E.

From 04 - Pulmonary Function Testing, 03 - Lung Physiology and 02 - Gas Exchange and Hypoxia. The PFT lecture lists early interstitial lung disease as a cause of an isolated DLCO drop, before there is enough fibrosis to cause restriction. The fall in DLCO is therefore early, not "only in very late stages", which makes E the false statement.

  • A: true. Parenchymal restriction is marked by a reduced DLCO, which is what separates it from extraparenchymal restriction.
  • C: true. By Fick's law, a thickened barrier slows diffusion; fibrosis is the example the lecture gives.
  • D: true. Scarring also destroys capillaries, which reduces the surface area and blood volume available to take up CO. The notes imply this rather than stating it.
  • B: true. At high flow during exercise, transfer becomes diffusion-limited. The lecture pairs ILD with hypoxemia on exercise; a scarred bed cannot recruit capillaries, so DLCO rises less than normal.

stem: The features of interstitial pulmonary fibrosis typically include all of the following expect:

options.html: prominent cough productive of copious amounts of purulent sputum

answer:
The correct answer is B.

From 05 - Interstitial Causes of Dyspnea. IPF presents with progressive dyspnea, a dry cough, bibasilar inspiratory crackles (almost always) and clubbing. Spirometry is restrictive with a reduced DLCO, and the CXR shows lines and nodules, mostly subpleural. Copious purulent sputum is a feature of an airway and infection disease such as bronchiectasis or CF, not of a fibrosing interstitium. B is the exception.

  • C: the thickened blood-gas barrier lowers DLCO.
  • D: bibasilar "velcro" crackles.
  • E: the reticular or nodular subpleural opacities described in the note.

The correct answer is E.

stem: What is the risk of having a baby with CF if mom has CF and her partner is a carrier?

options.html: A woman with CF can't conceive

answer:
The correct answer is B.

From 07 - Cystic Fibrosis. CF is autosomal recessive. The mother has CF, so she carries two mutant alleles and every child receives one mutant allele from her. The carrier partner passes his mutant allele half the time. The child is therefore affected (two mutant alleles) with probability 50% and a carrier otherwise.

  • A (25%): the risk when both parents are carriers, which is the figure the lecture gives.
  • C and D: would need the partner to pass the mutant allele more often than half the time, or to be affected himself (100%).
  • E: the lecture says women with CF have impaired fertility from thick, hostile cervical mucus, but are "not necessarily infertile". It is men who almost always lack a vas deferens.

stem: What is not true of CFTR?

options.html: it aids in regeneration and promotes wound healing
it can act as a tumour suppressor
it is expressed in every organ
You need a lot of working CFTR to prevent the complications of cystic fibrosis

answer:
The correct answer is E.

From 07 - Cystic Fibrosis and the CF mutation-class panel of 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease. The chart states it outright: not much working CFTR is needed to prevent CF complications. That is why milder mutations with some residual function spare the pancreas, and why modulators that restore even partial function help. E is the false statement.

  • A: true. CFTR is an ATP-gated chloride channel, a salt channel.
  • B: true. The lecture lists wound healing among CFTR's other functions.
  • C: true. It acts as a tumour suppressor; CF carries ↑ adenocarcinoma risk.
  • D: true in the lecture's sense. CFTR is in all epithelial cells: lung, pancreas, sweat glands, liver, gut, testes, brain.

stem: What is not a pathological finding in the lungs of CF patients?
answer:
The correct answer is E.

From 07 - Cystic Fibrosis. Thick, inspissated mucus obstructs the small airways. The lecture's list of lower-tract consequences includes atelectasis, emphysema, chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, pneumonia, cavitary lesions, respiratory failure and right heart failure / cor pulmonale. Atherosclerosis is a systemic arterial disease and appears nowhere on that list, so E is not a CF lung finding.

  • A (atelectasis): distal to mucus plugs.
  • B (bronchiectasis): from repeated infection, as the bronchial cartilage breaks down.
  • C (abscess): biofilm infection (S. aureus, Pseudomonas) leads to cavitation.
  • D (pulmonary artery hypertrophy): chronic hypoxic vasoconstriction produces pulmonary hypertension and remodelling. That is the path to cor pulmonale.

stem: Which is not a GI-related complication of CF?
answer:
The correct answer is G.

From 07 - Cystic Fibrosis. CFTR sits in GI epithelium, so the lecture's GI list is long:

  • A: exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, from ducts blocked by mucus, present from birth in most patients.
  • B: CF-related diabetes, i.e. endocrine insufficiency (25% of children, 50% of adults).
  • C: pancreatitis, from the same ductal obstruction.
  • D: DIOS, the adult meconium-ileus equivalent, with RLQ pain mistaken for appendicitis.
  • E: focal biliary cirrhosis, gallstones and portal hypertension.
  • F: rectal prolapse, from chronic malabsorption and diarrhea.

G is the odd one out. The digit sign in CF is clubbing, which the lecture files under skeletal changes (hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy), not GI. “Sausage” swollen digits are dactylitis, a feature of psoriatic arthritis and sickle cell disease.

stem: A patient breathing room air has a PaO2 of 65 and a PaCO2 of 60. The alveolar‑arterial gradient is oxygen is:
answer:
The correct answer is B.

From 02 - Gas Exchange and Hypoxia. On room air, PIO2 = 0.21 × (760 − 47) ≈ 150 mm Hg. With the lecture's alveolar gas equation, PAO2 = 150 − PaCO2/0.8 = 150 − 60/0.8 = 150 − 75 = 75, so the A–a gradient = 75 − 65 = 10. The Schulich shortcut, PaCO2 × 1.25, gives the same 10. Ten is not offered. 13 (B) is the nearest option and is what the full alveolar gas equation gives, since its extra FiO2 term makes the CO2 factor about 1.2: 150 − 60 × 1.2 ≈ 78, and 78 − 65 ≈ 13. Either way the gradient is normal (under age/4 + 4). With a PaCO2 of 60, this is pure hypoventilation.

  • A, C, D: too high for any version of the equation.
  • E (4): too low.

stem: A 40 year old male takes an overdose of barbiturates and is brought to the Emergency Department semi‑comatose with respirations of 12/min, blood pressure 120/80, pulse 76/min. answer:
The correct answer is A.

From 04 - Blood Gases Interpretation and 02 - Gas Exchange and Hypoxia. The pH of 7.32 is acidemia, and a PaCO2 of 50 explains it, so this is a primary respiratory acidosis. Is it acute? The rule for acute respiratory acidosis is HCO3 up 1 per 10 rise in PaCO2, so expect about 25. The measured 24 means the kidneys have not compensated yet (that takes about 24 hours). The pH fits too: a fall of about 0.08 for a 10 mm Hg rise. The A–a gradient is 150 − 50/0.8 = 87.5, minus 79, giving about 8, which is normal. That is pure hypoventilation: barbiturates cause CNS depression.

  • B, D, E: a metabolic acidosis needs a low HCO3. Here it is normal.
  • C: chronic compensation (HCO3 up 3 per 10) would give about 27 and a nearly normal pH.

Bronchiole artery (high pressure) from distortion and local destruction

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Due to the anatomical changes at the airway level of the blood vessels that supply the airways. A is not related to bronchiectasis; B is associated with a pulmonary abscess and does not usually contribute to infectious causes of exacerbations; D usually does not occur in bronchiectasis.

stem: What infection is NOT usually associated with necrotizing lesions causing hemoptysis?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

From 01 - Hemoptysis and 02 - Pneumonia. Mycoplasma is an atypical organism. It causes an interstitial pneumonia with patchy inflammation of the alveolar walls, an insidious onset and a non-productive cough. It does not destroy parenchyma, so it does not form necrotizing or cavitating lesions.

  • A (M. tuberculosis): the most common cause of cavitary lung disease. It bleeds through capillary leak or erosion into a pulmonary artery (Rasmussen aneurysm).
  • C (Klebsiella): listed among lung-abscess pathogens and in alcohol-associated pneumonia.
  • D (S. aureus): the first-listed abscess pathogen. MRSA is also flagged in abscess plus pneumonia.

answer:
The correct answer is D.

From 01 - Hemoptysis. Autoimmune lung disease has several radiographic faces, and the lecture describes each option:

  • A (whiteout): diffuse alveolar hemorrhage from pulmonary capillaritis (e.g. in vasculitis) can look like a complete whiteout and can be life-threatening.
  • B (pneumonia features): alveolar hemorrhage fills airspaces like an infection. The lecture separates the two by serial lavage: returns get more bloody with DAH and clear with pneumonia.
  • C (cavitary disease): granulomatosis with polyangiitis is the vasculitis most often causing cavitary lung disease.

Each is a real presentation, so D. The treatment is steroids for the autoimmune cause, not antibiotics.

stem: What can a bronchoscopy help in terms of hemoptysis management?

options.html: Serial washings to help identify diffuse alveolar hemorrhage

answer:
The correct answer is E.

From 01 - Hemoptysis. The lecture gives bronchoscopy several jobs in hemoptysis:

  • A: direct visualisation localises the bleeding site, the first goal in hemoptysis.
  • B: washings/BAL can be cultured, separating infectious causes (bronchitis, pneumonia, TB, aspergillus) from others.
  • C: serial BAL identifies diffuse alveolar hemorrhage. The return gets more bloody with each washout, the opposite of pneumonia.
  • D: it allows site-directed treatment, such as argon plasma coagulation of a bleeding tumour, and guides next steps (embolisation, surgery).

Each is a real role, so E. CT gives anatomy and arteriography can embolise; neither offers all four.

stem: Massive hemoptysis management often does NOT include which?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

From 01 - Hemoptysis. Massive hemoptysis, a quick bleed of around 100 mL per hour, is an airway emergency. Management starts with ABCs: protect the airway (intubation, an endobronchial blocker), lie the patient on the bleeding side, reverse anticoagulants and consider tranexamic acid. That care belongs in an ICU, not an outpatient clinic. CT is useful, since it localizes the bleed and guides the radiologist, but it is done urgently while the patient is in hospital, never booked as an outpatient scan. So D is the answer.

  • A (ICU): needed for airway protection and resuscitation.
  • B (bronchial artery embolization): arteriography localizes the bleed and treats it by embolization.
  • C (surgical resection): the last resort, for example in tumour or vasculitis.

stem: Where do the majority of nosebleeds occur?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

From In Class - Epistaxis and the Rhinology chart in 07 - Radiology. Most nosebleeds, about 90%, are anterior, from Kiesselbach's plexus in Little's area of the anterior septum. There the anterior ethmoid, superior labial, sphenopalatine and greater palatine branches anastomose under thin mucosa, exposed to drying air and fingers. These are the bleeds seen in younger patients, controlled with pressure and cautery.

  • B (posterior septum): Woodruff's plexus, sphenopalatine territory. Less common, but more severe, and seen in older and hypertensive patients.
  • A (cribriform plate), D (olfactory mucosa): the olfactory roof of the cavity, not a vascular watershed prone to bleeding.

From In Class - Epistaxis and the Rhinology chart in 07 - Radiology. The notes group epistaxis causes as local and systemic. Local causes are trauma, including nasal fracture and nose picking, plus foreign body, tumour, drugs such as cocaine, inflammation and dryness. Systemic causes are coagulopathy, hypertension, atherosclerosis, HHT and GPA.

  • B (nasal trauma), C (cocaine): local.
  • D (coagulopathy), E (atherosclerosis): systemic. Stiff, fragile vessels bleed more and stop less, which is part of why posterior bleeds cluster in the elderly.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

From the stepwise plan in 07 - Radiology. The ladder specifies unilateral silver nitrate cautery, applied outside in. The septal cartilage has no blood supply of its own and is fed by the mucoperichondrium on both sides. Cauterizing opposite points at once can devascularize the cartilage between them and cause a septal perforation. So the statement is false: treat the bleeding side, and if the other side needs it, come back later. The perforation mechanism comes from general principles; the notes only give the unilateral rule.

  • A (true): contradicts the "unilateral" instruction in the management plan.

stem: True or False: It is sometimes necessary to pack the nose bilaterally to stop an anterior bleed.
answer:
The correct answer is A.

From In Class - Epistaxis and the stepwise plan in 07 - Radiology. After ABCs, reversing coagulopathy, 10–15 minutes of firm anterior pressure and unilateral silver-nitrate cautery, the next step is packing, whether nasal tampon or ribbon gauze. The notes do not discuss bilateral packing. The logic is mechanical: the septum is thin and mobile, and a pack on the bleeding side alone can push it across without compressing the vessel. Packing the other side as well gives counter-pressure, clamping the septal bleeding point between two packs. So the statement is true: sometimes needed, not routine.

  • B (false): would mean one pack always suffices, which fails when the septum deviates away from it.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Lung Mechanics, Obstructive Disease & the Upper Airway
lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: Which of the following describes the correct order of the structures in the respiratory system?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

From 05 - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory System, 02 - Anatomy of the Lungs and Thorax and 01 - Histology. Air passes from the pharynx through the laryngeal inlet into the larynx and "then down into the trachea". The trachea descends from the larynx and bifurcates into the primary and then lobar bronchi. The bronchi branch into bronchioles (terminal, then respiratory) and end in the acinus. So the order is pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles.

  • A: puts the trachea above the larynx.
  • B: puts the larynx above the pharynx and the bronchioles before the bronchi.
  • C: starts at the trachea, below both the pharynx and the larynx.

stem: You asked to manage a 52 year old non-smoking man with a 12 month history of progressive exertional dyspnea and non-productive coughing. Review of systems is negative and he has no comorbidities. Physical exam demonstrates bibasilar crackles and clubbing. PFTs demonstrate FEV1 70%, FEV1/FVC ratio 78%, TLC 65% and DLCO 65%. answer:
The correct answer is A.

Refer back to PFT asynchronous learning

From 04 - Pulmonary Function Testing and the IPF column of 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease. Work the PFTs in order. The FEV1/FVC is 78%, at least 0.7, so there is no obstruction. TLC is 65%, under 80%, so this is restriction. DLCO is reduced, placing the restriction within the parenchyma. The clinical picture matches the chart's IPF profile: insidious progressive dyspnea at 40–70, a non-productive cough, bibasilar inspiratory crackles, clubbing, and honeycombing on imaging.

  • D (pulmonary edema): an airspace/fluid process, without 12 months of fibrosis, traction bronchiectasis and honeycombing.

stem: When we inhale:

options.html: The pressure decreases and intrapleural pressure increases
Both alveolar pressure and intrapleural pressure increases
Both alveolar pressure and intrapleural pressure decreases
Alveolar pressure increases and intrapleural pressure decreases

answer:
The correct answer is C.

See the mechanics of breathing physiology lecture.

From 03 - Lung Physiology - Ventilation. Inspiration is active. The diaphragm and external intercostals expand the thoracic cavity, making intrapleural pressure more negative (a decrease, from about −5 cm H2O toward −8). The lung expands with it, and alveolar (intrapulmonary) pressure falls to about −1 below atmospheric, so air flows in. Both pressures fall.

  • A: intrapleural pressure does not rise on inspiration. It only approaches atmospheric in forced expiration or pneumothorax.
  • B: both rising describes forced expiration.
  • D: alveolar pressure rises only in expiration, when air is pushed out.

Breathing a mixture of 21% O2 and 79% of helium

The correct answer is D.

Inhaling cigarette smoking will cause airway muscles to spasm, increase mucus secretion and lead to narrowing of the air way and increase resistance. Increase lung volumes, and sympathetic stimulation will lead to increase in the airway diameter and decrease the resistance. High altitude has nothing to do with airway calibers and resistance. stem: Pulmonary surfactant:

options.html: Increases the surface tension of the alveolar lining liquid
Is secreted by type I alveolar epithelial cells
Increases the work required to expand the lung
Helps to prevent transudation of the fluid from the capillaries into the alveolar space

answer:
The correct answer is E.

From 03 - Lung Physiology - Ventilation and 01 - Histology of the Lungs and Airway. Surfactant has four listed functions: it lowers surface tension, raises compliance, reduces alveolar edema and aids O2 diffusion. High surface tension would draw fluid from the capillaries into the alveoli, and surfactant opposes that. Without it, as in infant respiratory distress syndrome, the alveoli flood and collapse. So E is true.

  • A: surfactant decreases surface tension (Laplace), keeping small alveoli from collapsing.
  • B: it is secreted by type 2 pneumocytes. Type 1 cells form the thin gas-exchange surface.
  • C: the lecture describes it as a lipid film at the air-liquid interface. It is mainly phospholipid, not simply a protein.
  • D: by raising compliance it decreases the work of expanding the lung.

answer:
The correct answer is E.

No muscle group is required for unforced expiration. The lungs contract through elastic recoil, gravity that lowers and compresses the thoracic cage, and relaxation of the diaphragm to relieve high abdominal pressures. During forced expiration, the abdominal muscles and internal/innermost intercostal muscles are employed.

Perfusion is greatest at the base of the lung
The V/Q ratio is smallest at the apex of the lung
Pneumonia is likely to increase the overall V/Q ratio of the lung

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Perfusion is greatest at the base of the lung. Ventilation is also greatest at the base of the lung; however perfusion is much greater which leads to a low V/Q ratio at the base of the lung. The apex of the lung generally has a high V/Q ratio due its reduced ventilation, and significantly reduced perfusion. Pneumonia is a disease that damages your alveoli (through fluid or pus accumulation) and drastically lowers the ventilation, thus the V/Q ratio is likely to decrease in patients with Pneumonia.

stem: Taylor is in the middle of a very exhausting 2-km sprint on a hot summer afternoon. Which of the following likely describes the change that may occur to her hemoglobin dissociation curve?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

The curve will be right-shifted. During exercise, Taylor is producing a larger amount of CO2, which dissolves in the blood and contributes to increasing acidity. Her muscle bed is in greater need of oxygen due to exertion – Hemoglobin must be more “willing” to offload this oxygen to her tissues. When the curve is right shifted due to Increased CO2, acidity and temperature – hemoglobin has a lesser affinity for oxygen at a given PaO2. A left shifted curve would be seen in environments where there is decreased CO2, alkalosis and decreased temperature.

stem: A 40-year-old patient with worsening shortness of breath and a concerning spirometry test undergoes a CT scan revealing developing emphysema (alveolar fluid collection leading to alveolar hypoxia) localized to a single bronchopulmonary segment in the patient’s right lung. If the patient were to undergo a perfusion test of the various segments of the right lung which of the following would most likely be seen?

options.html: Increased perfusion to the diseased bronchopulmonary segment and decreased perfusion to other bronchopulmonary segments in the right lung
Decreased perfusion to the diseased bronchopulmonary segment and increased perfusion to other bronchopulmonary segments in the right lung
Overall decreased perfusion among all bronchopulmonary segments but significant reduction in the diseased bronchopulmonary segment
Overall increased perfusion among all bronchopulmonary segments but significant increase in the diseased bronchopulmonary segment

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Hypoxemic Vasoconstriction is a homeostatic mechanism that redirects pulmonary blood flow to areas of high ventilation. Pulmonary vasculature around diseased alveoli with low ventilation will constrict this will redirect blood flow to other areas of the lung with better ventilation. In this situation we can expect the patient to have reduced perfusion to the diseased bronchopulmonary segment, and increased perfusion to other bronchopulmonary segments of the right lung. While in the short term this maximizes oxygenation of the blood flow, this can also contribute to pulmonary blood flow in the long term.

The correct answer is B.

The equation for PAO2 is (FiO2 * (Patm – PH2O) – (PaCO2 / Qresp). Increasing FIO2, Patm, or Qresp would increase the calculated value for PAO2. By breathing in 100% pure oxygen, FIO2 goes from 0.21 (atmospheric oxygen fraction) to 1.0, and subsequently increases PAO2.

stem: Which of the following changes will increase hemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

For the most part, hemoglobin affinity to oxygen “makes sense”. During a time of physical activity / exercise, CO2 increases, pH decreases, and temperature increased. All of these result in hemoglobin having a reduced affinity for oxygen, allowing the delivery of oxygen to muscles. An increase in DPG also reduces affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen. Conversely, decreasing the temperature, decreasing the CO2, or increasing the pH increases hemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen.

stem: Which option correctly describes a phenomenon associated with lung physiology?

options.html: “Absolute deadspace” occurs when ventilation to a portion of the lung is nonexistent.
Passive exhalation requires the contraction of the abdominal muscles and the inner intercostal muscles.
Hypoxic vasoconstriction is a means by which the perfusion to a poorly ventilated area of the lung decreases.
Pulmonary embolism and pulmonary edema primarily result in decreased ventilation.

answer:
The correct answer is C.

In hypoxic vasoconstriction, a lack of ventilation to an area (caused by consolidation, for example), results in a reduction of bloodflow to that area. Absolute deadspace occurs when perfusion to a portion of the lung is non-existent. Passive exhalation does not require any muscle contractions; the elastic recoil of the alveoli drives this. Pulmonary embolism leads to increased perfusion.

stem: A patient presents to the clinic with a severe localized injury to their lower thoracic vertebrae at the level of the diaphragm. The physician notes although the patient seems to be paralyzed below that level the patient is still capable of breathing in and out. Which of the following explains why the patient is able to keep breathing without issue despite a spinal injury at the level of the diaphragm?

options.html: Even though the patient’s innervation to the diaphragm may be injured they can rely on their external intercostal muscles for inspiration
Even though the patient’s innervation to the diaphragm may be injured they can rely on their internal intercostal muscles for inspiration
Inspiration is a passive process and does not require any external muscles but relies on long recoil
The diaphragm is innervated by spinal nerves originating at a higher level than the thorax

answer:
The correct answer is D.

The diaphragm is a muscle that sits inferior to the lung, and plays an essential role in inspiration – when it contracts inferiorly it expands the thoracic cage vertically and allows air to enter the lung. The external intercostal muscles also assist in inspiration (the external intercostals assist in forced expiration). Inspiration is thus not an active process. The diaphragm is supplied by bilateral phrenic nerves that originate from C3,C4,C5, so a spinal injury at the thoracic level would not affect the innervation to the diaphragm.

The patient’s TLC is significantly reduced at 65% of the expected volume, which suggests a lung volume restriction. stem: Which of the following statements is correct?

options.html: Inhaled drug particles with a smaller particle size have a greater percentage of deposition within the lungs
A majority of the inhaled medications is deposited within the lungs
Inhaled drugs with high first pass metabolism generally are less of a concern for adverse side effects
Dry powder inhaler devices are recommended for patient with shortness of breath

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Inhaled drugs with higher first pass metabolism are generally safer in that there is less of a risk for adverse side effects. This is because the majority of the inhaled drug is digested and travels through systemic circulation to be deactivated by the liver. Inhaled drugs that have low first pass metabolism won’t be as metabolized and this could lead to a toxic dose in the body contributing to adverse side effects. Inhaled drug particles should not be too large (>10 micrometers) to prevent deposition in the mouth/oropharynx, however they should not be too small otherwise they are inhaled into the lung and then exhaled without being deposited. Dry powder inhaler devices require patients to take forceful inspiration at high flow rates, thus it would not be appropriate for patients with breathing problems.

The correct answer is D.

stem: One day while taking the bus to the grocery store, you strike up a conversation with a fellow commuter. You mention that you’re a first-year medical student currently studying respirology, and she starts asking you some questions about her asthma medications. She tells you that she’s been using Salbutamol (a SABA), and she’s been using it for awhile but it no longer seems to help with her symptoms despite frequent use. She is a 57-year-old female who is recently unemployed and having trouble finding work because of Covid. If you were her primary care physician, what next step would you recommend?

options.html: Continue salbutamol and increase dose frequency.
Deprescribe salbutamol and prescribe a LABA (salmeterol)
Deprescribe salbutamol and prescribe a LABA and corticosteroid (Prednisone)
Deprescribe salbutamol and prescribe a monoclonal antibody (Omalizumab)

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Salbutamol can lead to tachyphylaxis (tolerance). If this occurs, the SABA is converted to a LABA. Also, LABAs are most effective when used in combination with corticosteroids, such as prednisone. Thus, your new commuter friend should benefit from double therapy of a LABA and corticosteroid. While she may benefit from a monoclonal antibody, these tend to be very expensive. Since she’s recently unemployed with no future prospects, it would not be financially responsible to prescribe her with monoclonal antibody therapy.

options.html: Airways are constricted but the alveoli are open
Alveoli have fluid accumulation and the airways are not obstructed
Alveoli and airways show signs of fluid accumulation

stem: Which of the following is a correct statement regarding central and peripheral chemoreceptors?

options.html: Peripheral receptors receive a high venous flow to measure blood pH.
Central chemoreceptors measure blood pH directly from the cerebral blood vessels.
Central chemoreceptors measure pH changes in the CSF arising from diffusion of
Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid arch are innervated by the glossopharyngeal Nerve.

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Peripheral chemoreceptors receive a high arterial (not venous) flow to measure blood pH. Central chemoreceptors measure blood pH directly from the CSF, however CO2 (not bicarbonate) diffuses into the CSF. Elevated CO2 levels passes through the blood brain barrier to enter the CSF.

stem: Which of the following receptors plays the largest role in ventilation and breathing?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Central chemoreceptors generally have the most influence in the control of ventilation and breathing. Irritant and pulmonary stretch receptors (both lung receptors) also play a role in responding to irritants and preventing over-inflation, respectively. Baroreceptors generally have the least influence in moderating ventilation and breathing.

stem: Taylor is preparing for a class presentation and is very anxious. She begins hyperventilating. Which of the following changes is expected as a result of hyperventilation? Select THREE answers.
answer:
The correct answer is A, D, E.

With hyperventilation, there is an increased rate of gas exchange where oxygen is being dissolved in the blood and CO2 is expelled out of the lungs. Thus, Taylor will show increased oxygen content in the blood, and decreased CO2. Hyperventilation is also accompanied by alkalosis. Under standard circumstances, CO2 dissolves in the plasma leading to increased bicarbonate dissociation (contributing to acidity). When CO2 is low, due to increased clearance of CO2 from the blood, this leads to alkalosis of the blood.

stem: Which of the following situations would likely result in decreased ventilation?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Decreased arterial carbon dioxide is often accompanied by alkalosis – decreasing the rate of breathing would allow more CO2 to accumulate in the blood and normalize the pH without being immediately cleared by the lungs. Heavy exercise, higher altitudes (lower oxygen concentration), and clinical acidosis all lead to increased ventilation.

stem: Ventilation rates increase as PaCO2 increases, as PaO2 decreases, and as pH decreases. The increase in ventilation is the result of various sensors that detect changes in these values. Which relationship below is correct?

options.html: Changes in PaCO2 are detected primarily by the central chemoreceptors
Changes in blood pH are detected primarily by the peripheral chemoreceptors
Changes in PaO2 are detected primarily by the peripheral chemoreceptors
All of the above are correct

answer:
The correct answer is E.

The central chemoreceptor primary responds to increased PaCO2 levels to elevate respiratory rates. The peripheral receptors respond to decreases in O2 and decreases in pH (increased acidity) to elevate respiratory rates.

stem: Consider a patient with diabetic ketoacidosis. Blood tests indicate that the pH of this patient’s blood is 7.30 (normal = 7.38-7.42) and the PaCO2 is 42 mmHg (normal = 38-42 mmHg). What is the likely physiological response and cause of this response?

options.html: Increased respiratory rate due to signals from the central chemoreceptor
Decreased respiratory rate due to signals from the central chemoreceptor
Increased respiratory rate due to signals from the peripheral chemoreceptors
Decreased respiratory rate due to signals from the peripheral chemoreceptors

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Acidosis will lead to an increase in respiratory rate, mainly due to signals to the peripheral chemoreceptors. The central receptor does not respond to blood pH levels, but instead responds to pH of the CSF; excess carbon dioxide diffuses into the CSF, increasing the acidity.

A 24-year-old patient arrives at the ER with signs of hypoxemia. Their arterial blood gas

stem: What is the most likely cause of this acid-base problem?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

The patient’s pH reflects acidosis. The patient’s PaCO2 is significantly elevated, however the HCO3- seems to be on the slightly higher of normal. This points towards a respiratory acidosis from hypoventilation, with a metabolic response (kidney retaining bicarbonate ions). Within a few hours the bicarbonate ions will likely elevate to compensate for the acidosis.

The correct answer is B.

The patient’s O2 level is significantly decreased. Their A-a gradient can be calculated by first calculating the PAO2 from the PaCO2 = 150-1.25*(80) = 50. options.html: pH = 7.48; PaO2 = 65 mmHg; PaCO2 = 34 mmHg; HCO3- = 21 meq/L
pH = 7.49; PaO2 = 65 mmHg; PaCO2 = 41 mmHg; HCO3- = 22 meq/L
pH = 7.50; PaO2 = 65 mmHg; PaCO2 = 60 mmHg; HCO3- = 26 meq/L
pH = 7.16; PaO2 = 55 mmHg; PaCO2 = 72 mmHg; HCO3- = 28 meq/L
pH = 7.32; PaO2 = 65 mmHg; PaCO2 = 59 mmHg; HCO3- = 27 meq/L

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Alkalosis implies a pH greater than 7.45. In respiratory alkalosis, increased respiratory rates results in a decrease in PaCO2 and a concomitant increase in pH. The correct answer is A, F, I.

Lung abscess caused by anaerobic pneumonia - treat with incision
Community acquired pneumonia - treat with antibiotics

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Left-sided heart failure can cause pulmonary edema, an interstitial and alveolar cause of dyspnea. This can present with Kerley B lines on Chest X-ray and shortness of breath. The treatment for this heart failure is typically ACE-inhibitors and beta-blockers (among other medications)

stem: A 80-year-old patient presents to your clinic with concerns of worsening shortness of breath over the past couple of months. Upon taking a history, there is no significant travel history or exposures. A physical exam reveals clubbing of the fingernails, and a CXR reveals “honeycombing” of the lung in the sub pleural spaces. The physician has a high degree of certainty of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). Which of the following is the next step?

options.html: Perform a biopsy to confirm IPF
Perform a CT scan to confirm IPF
Perform a spirometry test to confirm IPF

answer:
The correct answer is A.

A diagnosis of IPF can be made based on clinical symptoms if there is a high degree of certainty, thus further testing is often not required. The patient’s symptoms (clubbing, dyspnea, honeycombing) are very indicative of IPF. Further testing (taking a biopsy and interpreting) would be appropriate in patients with uncertain symptoms or radiological findings.

stem: Which of the following statements is correct regarding Sarcoidosis?

options.html: Sarcoidosis commonly presents in the elderly population
People with sarcoidosis are often very symptomatic and show physical signs upon examination (eg, clubbing)
Patients with sarcoidosis commonly present with normal lung function
Increasing stages of sarcoidosis (radiologic stage 1-4) is associated with an increase in mortality and morbidity.

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Sarcoidosis is more common in younger patients and does not particularly affect the elderly like IPF. People with IPF are often very symptomatic (signs of dyspnea and chest pain + clubbing). The radiographic stages of sarcoidosis are not meant to be interpreted in a linear fashion where one stage progresses into another.

stem: What is the primary purpose of a lung biopsy when a patient is suspected to have sarcoidosis in the lungs?

options.html: To assess the likelihood of the sarcoidosis progression from Stage 1 to Stage 4
To identify the pathogenic organism causing the infection
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis must be ruled out
A clinical presentation of suspected sarcoidosis is not enough to establish a diagnosis

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Sarcoidosis cannot be diagnosed purely clinically, but instead is diagnose clinicopathologically. In sarcoidosis, patients do not progress along the different stages, making option A false. Sarcoidosis is not an infection, so option B is false. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is a diagnosis of exclusion, so it would not be ruled out with a lung biopsy, making option C false.

Both patient’s spirometry tests display a normal FEV1/FVC ratio, however Taylor’s Total Lung Capacity and Residual Volume is significantly reduced. Taylor and Drake’s CT is shown below. Which of the following is true?

Taylor and Drake both likely have sarcoidosis
Taylor likely has idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis while Drake likely has sarcoidosis
Taylor likely has sarcoidosis while Drake likely has idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Taylor’s symptoms (long standing dyspnea, reduced lung capacity with preserved FEV1/FVC) are indicative of interstitial pulmonary fibrosis. Her CT scan also displays honeycombs in the subpleural regions of the lung. Drake’s lack of symptoms and normal spirometry tests are more in aligning with a diagnosis of sarcoidosis. In addition, on his CT scan, sarcoidosis often appears as a nodular disease in the medial regions of the lung.

stem: As a physician, you are trying to distinguish between two potential diagnoses: COPD and Asthma. Which of the following values in a spirometer test would be MOST helpful in distinguishing between the two?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Asthma is a variable obstructive lung disease that is responsive to bronchodilators. Patients who are experiencing an episode of bronchospasm can take a bronchodilator and ease the resistance in their airways restoring and FEV1/FVC value. Patients with COPD have irreversible lung damage and their airways won’t have a significant response to bronchodilators to restore FEV1/FVC back to normal values. COPD and asthma are both obstructive airway disease thus peak expiratory flow may be diminished, while TLC, and DLCO will likely be unaffected.

stem: You are a third-year clerk in your family medicine rotation seeing a patient who presents with complaints of a cough. She tells you that the cough comes and goes but has been more persistent lately. Her history is unremarkable for exposure risks, and today’s PFT results appear normal. What test would you order to confirm your suspected diagnosis?

options.html: Prescribe a short-acting beta agonist like salbutamol for the patient to take the next time she develops a cough to see if her symptoms resolve.
Have the patient inhale methacholine to constrict the lungs, and then repeat a PFT.
Repeat a PFT later when the patient has a cough to make the diagnosis.
Culture the patient’s sputum to rule out an infection – asthma is a diagnosis of exclusion.
Repeat the PFT test after administering Ventolin to dilate the airways of the lungs.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

This patient’s clinical picture points toward asthma (intermittent obstruction, normal PFT test today), and the patient is likely presenting without symptoms today because she is not currently having an asthma exacerbation. In these situations, a methacholine challenge test can be performed to confirm a diagnosis - methacholine is slowly and incrementally administered and the patient’s PFT tests are repeatedly performed to observe a decrease in lung function.

stem: Which patient below is considered to have “massive hemoptysis”?

options.html: Aaron, who has expectorated 250 mL of blood over the past 2 hours
Bobby, who has expectorated 400 mL of blood over the past 24 hours
Chris, who has expectorated 700 mL of blood over the past 48 hours
David, who has expectorated 500 mL of blood over the past 72 hours

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Aaron has expectorated an average of 125 mL per hour for two hours. More than 100 mL of blood in a single hour is a massive hemoptysis. Additionally, expectorating 650 mL in a 24-hour period also indicates massive hemoptysis.

stem: Which statement on the treatment of various etiologies of hemoptysis is true?

options.html: Bronchoscopic techniques are valuable for diagnosis but not for treatment
With any hemoptysis, the patient should be seated upright
Surgical resection is the first-line therapy for neoplastic etiologies of hemoptysis
Arterial embolization is a process to occlude damaged blood vessels upstream of the bleed

answer:
The correct answer is D.

In arterial embolization, a plug is inserted upstream of a damaged blood vessel, preventing future blood loss. Bronchoscopic techniques are valuable for diagnosis with increases uses for treatment. In patients with hemoptysis, they are positioned in a later decubitus position with the “bleeding side down”. Surgical resection is an invasive procedure that is performed as last-line therapy.

A 40-year-old man presents to the ER coughing up blood with complaints of dyspnea and chest

pain. The patient’s previous history shows a history of epistaxis, skin lesions, and hematuria

(blood in urine). A prior V/Q scan at the hospital also shows several lung compartments as

physiologic dead spaces. A chest X ray conducted at the ER visit shows diffuse alveolar markings

across both lungs.

stem: Which of the following pathologies best explains the patient’s symptoms?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Diffuse Alveolar Hemorrhage resulting from vasculitis of the capillary beds is the most likely presentation. The systemic involvement of bleeding in many organ systems and the V/Q scan point towards a perfusion problem. Furthermore the diffuse alveolar marking is consistent with the diffuse alveolar hemorrhage x-ray presentation.

The mass was 5.5 cm in diameter (in the greatest dimension), with local involvement with a single ipsilateral hilar lymph node, indicated by positron-emission tomography with 18-fluorodeoxyglucose. answer:
The correct answer is D.

Firstly, the patient’s lung mass has not metastasized to other tissues or organs, so the “M” staging is 0. The tumour size is between 5 and 7 cm is the greatest direction, indicating T3. With unilateral local lymph node involvement, the N stage is N1.

stem: Which statement regarding the malignancy of pulmonary nodules is true?

Larger nodules decrease the likelihood that a nodule is benign
Less dense nodules with a ground-glass appearance are more likely to be malignant
Lymphomas, granulomas, and hamartomas are malignant nodules

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Larger nodules are more likely to be malignant. Option A is false - calcification increases the likelihood that the nodule is benign. A patient with a large lung nodule and significant risk factors for lung cancer underwent a

CT/PET scan. The lung nodule indicates elevated metabolism. In addition, several regions of her

brain also indicate increased metabolism. A subsequent brain MRI shows no remarkable

findings.

stem: Which of the following is an appropriate next step?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

The lung nodule “lighting up” on a PET scan can be indicative of cancer – _cancerous cells have increased glucose uptake which is measured on a PET scan. Since the brain largely consumes glucose, this is not suggestive of a malignancy, furthermore the brain MRI scan detecting no abnormalities supports the need for no further testing. A lung biopsy can be performed to stage and determine the prognosis/treatment for the cancer.

stem: Which pre-school patient below has the greatest likelihood of having asthma during school?

options.html: A 3-year-old with 4 episodes of wheeze in the past year with a parent with asthma
A 3-year-old with 3 episodes of wheeze in the past year with allergic sensitization to food
A 3-year-old with 4 episodes of wheeze in the past year with eosinophilia
A 3-year-old with 4 episodes of wheeze in the past year with a parent with emphysema
A 3-year-old with 3 episodes of wheeze in the past year associated with bacterial pneumonia

answer:
The correct answer is A.

The predictive index of asthma applies to pre-school children who have had 4 episodes of wheeze in the past year. To predict if the child is likely to have asthma in school, one major criterion (parent with asthma, atopic dermatitis, or allergic sensitization of aeroallergens) OR two major criteria (wheezing apart from colds, eosinophilia, or allergic sensitization to foods) must be present.

stem: The management for asthma in children varies depending on the child’s age. Which statement below is true?

options.html: A 3-year-old with uncontrolled asthma should be prescribed prednisone
A 5-year-old with uncontrolled asthma should avoid taking LTRA
A 9-year-old with uncontrolled asthma should be prescribed prednisone as a last resort
A 13-year-old with uncontrolled asthma should avoid combination inhalers

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Pre-school children are generally not prescribed inhaled corticosteroids. LTRAs are prescribed to children after LABAs have not shown positive results. Children above the age of 6 can be prescribed inhaled corticosteroids if previous treatments have been ineffective. Lastly, above the age of 12, combination inhalers are commonly used.

stem: A 4-year-old patient arrives at your clinic with their mother. Their mother has concerns that the child may have asthma. Which investigations would you perform to arrive at a diagnosis? Select all that apply.

options.html: Perform a Pulmonary Function Test to measure FEV1/FVC
Documentation of wheezing or airflow obstruction by a HCP or parent
Perform a positive challenge test (methacholine challenge)
Documentation of reversibility of airflow obstruction (with SABA or ICS) from a HCP or parent
No investigations – asthma is only present in patients older than 6 years old

answer:
The correct answer is B, C, E.

For preschool asthma, it is not recommended to perform a pulmonary function test. The diagnostic criteria for preschool asthma (1-5 years old) includes 1) Documentation of airflow obstruction 2) Documentation of reversibility of airflow obstruction 3) No clinical evidence of an alternative diagnosis.

The asthma predictive index outlines major criteria and minor criteria (you must have at least 2 minor criteria) to reasonably predict a child will have school aged asthma. The minor criteria include wheezing apart from colds, eosinophilia, and allergic sensitization to milk, eggs, or peanuts.

stem: The CFTR gene is a pleiotropic gene, meaning that a mutation to the CFTR gene causes a variety of seemingly unrelated phenotypic effects. Which treatment option below is least valuable for a patient with a mutation in the CFTR gene leading to cystic fibrosis?

options.html: Inhalation of a hypertonic saline fluid
Postural drainage and percussion of the thoracic region

answer:
The correct answer is C.

The postural drainage and percussive therapy is an outdated therapy that carries the risk of aspiration of food particles. This is because patients with CF are more likely to suffer from improper functioning of the esophageal sphincter leading to GERD, nausea, and vomiting.

stem: Trikafta is a (relatively) novel drug that is highly effective in the treatment of cystic fibrosis (CF). What is the mechanism by which Trikafta alleviates symptoms of CF?

options.html: Trikafta involves inserting new DNA encoding wildtype CFTR protein into the genome
Trikafta involves modifying mutated CFTR DNA within the genome
Trikafta involves inserting new mRNA into cells with mutated CFTR genes
Trikafta involves restoring functionality to mutates CFTR proteins that fail to secrete chloride
Trikafta involves allowing cells to localize CFTR proteins to the cell membrane

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Trikafta is most valuable for patients with Cystic Fibrosis that possess the deltaF508 mutation (the most common mutation associated with CF). This mutated gene encodes a chlorine channel that is permanently closed, but Trikafta facilitates the opening of the channel.

Perform a sweat test; if positive, confirm with genotype analysis and then diagnose with cystic fibrosis
Perform direct DNA analysis to diagnose cystic fibrosis
Perform a fecal elastase and blood tests to diagnose cystic fibrosis

The correct answer is B.

The first step in investigating cystic fibrosis is a sweat test. A positive sweat test rules in cystic fibrosis but this must be confirmed with direct DNA analysis, as there are several disorders (celiac disease, G6PD deficiency, Kleinfelter’s) that can also result in a positive sweat test

Light’s criteria for pleural fluids considers the albumin, protein, and LDH levels of the pleural fluid and the blood serum. options.html: Issues with mechanical contraction of respiratory muscles

The primary reason for shortness of breath in patients with a significant build-up of pleural effusions involves ineffective diaphragm contraction which leads to breathing abnormalities. As the pleural fluid pushes against the diaphragm this contorts the tensionlength relationship.

However, the patient’s pleural LDH level is quite high relative to the serum level (80%). Which of the following statements is accurate to

options.html: The patient has an exudative process because the patient’s LDH level is very high
The patient has a transudative process because the patient’s LDH level is very high
The patient has an exudative process because the patient’s protein level is very low
The patient has a transudative process because the patient’s LDH and protein levels are low

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Patients with a pleural effusion who satisfy the Lights criteria can be classified as having an exudative process. The lung fields appear darker as you move inferiorly because of the effect of gravity on blood flow to the different regions of the lung. Blood will pool inferiorly, making perfusion at the lower lung lobes great than perfusion at the upper lung lobes.

Intrathoracic volume and diameter increases during inspiration
The internal intercostals contract during forced expiration

stem: What is the function of the mucociliary blanket?

options.html: Recruit macrophages to engulf foreign microorganisms and particulate matter
Decrease friction between the visceral and parietal pleura
Increase air flow by decreasing the radius of the airways
Prevent microorganisms and inhaled particulate matter from reaching the distal airways

answer:
The correct answer is D.

The mucociliary blanket is secreted from glands (in the bronchi) or produced by specialized epithelial cells (in the bronchioles). Its main function is to capture inhaled particulates and microorganisms. The cilia then “sweep” the mucus layer upwards, towards the epiglottis, so that it can be swallowed.

stem:
Match the muscle of the larynx with its function.

  1. Translational-adducts the vocal cords
  2. Pivot-adducts the vocal cords
  3. Abducts the vocal cords
  4. Lengthens the vocal cords
  5. Shortens the vocal cords
  6. Pulls epiglottis down
answer:
A – iv; B – v; C – iii; D – ii; E – i; F – vi.

From 05 - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory System. Each muscle acts on either the cricothyroid joint (pitch) or the cricoarytenoid joint (opening and closing):

  • A – iv: cricothyroid tilts the cricothyroid joint to lengthen the cords (↑ pitch). It is the only one supplied by the external laryngeal nerve.
  • B – v: vocalis/thyroarytenoid shorten the cords (↓ pitch).
  • C – iii: posterior cricoarytenoid rotates the vocal processes laterally. It is the only abductor.
  • D – ii: lateral cricoarytenoid rotates them medially, a pivot adduction.
  • E – i: interarytenoid slides the arytenoids together, a translational adduction synergistic with D.
  • F – vi: aryepiglottic pulls the epiglottis down to close the inlet in swallowing.

stem: What are the requirements of proper phonation?

options.html: Passive vibration of free mucosal edge of vocal folds

answer:
The correct answer is E.

All of the above are required for proper phonation.

Partly from the larynx section of Summary Notes - Anatomy. The anatomy notes cover the structure: the vocal ligament is covered by mucosa to form the vocal folds, the lateral cricoarytenoid adducts them, and the cricothyroid tenses them to raise pitch. Voice needs three things together:

  • A: the folds approximate (adduct) so that they close the glottis.
  • B: an expiratory airflow builds subglottic pressure beneath the closed folds.
  • C: that airflow sets the mucosal free edge passively vibrating. No muscle contracts for each cycle.

Remove any one and voice fails: open folds give a breathy voice, too little airflow gives no sound, and stiff scarred mucosa gives hoarseness. That makes E the answer. "Forced" overstates B, since conversational speech needs a controlled expiratory stream, not a forced one.

stem: Which of the following are complications from idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?

From the restrictive-disease chart in 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease and 05 - Interstitial Causes of Dyspnea. The prognosis row for IPF reads: rapid progression, mean survival 4–5 years, respiratory failure, pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale. All three follow one chain. Fibrosis thickens the barrier and stiffens the lung, and gas exchange fails. Chronic hypoxia constricts the pulmonary arterioles and the scarring destroys the capillary bed, producing pulmonary hypertension. The right ventricle then fails against that pressure, which is cor pulmonale. So E.

  • D (A and B): leaves out cor pulmonale, the end of the same chain.
  • A, B, C alone: each is true but incomplete.

stem: Which artery is highly associated with posterior epistaxis?

From In Class - Epistaxis and 05 - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory System. Posterior bleeds arise at Woodruff's plexus, where the sphenopalatine artery (maxillary artery, external carotid) enters the posterior nasal cavity. They drip down the throat, are rarely traumatic, are worse than anterior bleeds and cluster in elderly hypertensive patients. When packing fails, the surgical fix is sphenopalatine artery ligation.

  • B (facial artery): reaches the nose through the superior labial branch at the anterior septum (Kiesselbach's).

  • D (ophthalmic artery): the parent of both ethmoid arteries, supplying the roof rather than the posterior cavity.

answer:
The correct answer is D.

It can present as focused, local or diffused disease.

From 01 - Hemoptysis, with the bronchiectasis column in 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease. Bronchiectasis is permanent airway dilation after repeated infection or inflammation. Its causes include diffuse ones (CF, primary ciliary dyskinesia) and focal ones (an obstructing foreign body or tumour). The exam finding is localized crackles and the CXR findings are nonspecific, so "only diffuse" is false.

  • A (true): bronchitis is a diagnosis of exclusion, made after other infectious, parenchymal and alveolar causes are ruled out. The CXR is usually normal.
  • B (true): bleeding comes from damage to inflamed airways. Capillary leakage is more likely on blood thinners or with a smoking history.
  • C (true): repeated insults destroy the bronchial walls. This is why bronchiectasis is the most common cause of rapid, life-threatening hemoptysis.

  • B (coagulopathy): systemic. Reversing it is step 2 of management.
  • C (HHT): systemic. It is autosomal dominant, with malformed vessels in the nose and lungs.
  • E: fails because D is a local cause.

stem: What is true about lung masses?

Multiple nodules are often a sign of malignancy
Nodules less than 8mm have a lower chance of being malignant
It is often preferred to biopsy two different sites to diagnose and stage the cancer

(The note's "< 8cm" in the PET paragraph is a typo for mm.)

stem: Which of the following about lung volumes and capacities is correct?

options.html: The residual volume is the volume of gas that remains after max expiration and cannot be expelled
The tidal volume is air that enters the lung during normal breathing and is only air that is involved in gas exchange
The functional residual capacity is the air left after maximal expiration
The residual volume does not prevent the lung from collapsing after expiration

The correct answer is A.

stem: Alveolar surfactant acts to increase:
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Surfactant is a mixture of proteins and lipids manufactured by type 2 alveolar cells to reduce surface tension caused by water molecules in alveoli trying to collapse alveoli. Surfactant forms a monolayer on the alveoli to prevent water molecules from interacting. Reducing surface tension results in less negative pressure required to inflate the alveoli, therefore resulting in increased compliance. By reducing surface tension, the work of breathing is also reduced. A less known but important role of surfactant is also to reduce fluid entering alveoli by reducing the hydrostatic pressure in the tissues (a less negative interstitial space hydrostatic pressure)

stem: What is a normal FEV1/FVC ratio in a normal adult? FEV1 =forced expiratory volume in the 1st second, FVC= forced vital capacity. A) 0.6 B) 1 C) 0.8 D) 0.1
answer:
The correct answer is C.

The normal FEV1/FVC ratio is approximately 0.8. This ratio is extremely important because it can be a marker measured in suspected lung disease. In obstructive lung disease such as COPD or asthma, the FEV1/FVC ratio decreases (patient cannot expire as much in one second as a normal person). In restrictive lung disease, such as pulmonary fibrosis, the FEV1/FVC ratio is either normal or increases (both the FEV1 and FVC decrease).

stem: A patient in the ICU at sea level is breathing atmospheric air (21% O2) and you would like to know the amount of oxygen in the alveoli (PAO2, alveolar O2). The PACO2 is 40 mmHg. Using the alveolar oxgeyn equation, you calculate the PAO2 to be:
answer:
The correct answer is C.

The alveolar oxygen equation states that: PAO2 = inspired oxygen - oxygen consumed, where inspired O2 = PiO2. Therefore: PAO2 = PiO2 - oxygen consumed We can calcuate PiO2 at atmospheric levels as: PiO2 = (P(atm)- PH20)) x FiO2, where FiO2 is the fraction of inspired oxygen (0.21). PiO2 = (760 mmHg - 47 mmHg) x 0.21 PiO2 = 149.7 mmHg We calculate oxygen consumed through this equation: RQ=V(dot)CO2/V(dot)O2, where RQ (respiratory quotient) = 0.8 V(dot)CO2 is the same as PaCO2 (arterial concnetration of CO2), because most of the CO2 in our blood is the result of cellular metabolism. PaCO2 = 40 mmHg. Rearranging the first and second equations, we get: PAO2 = PiO2 – (PaCO2/RQ) PAO2 = 149.7 mmHg – (40 mmHg/0.8) PAO2 = 99.7 mmHg

stem: A patient comes to the ER with a pulmonary embolism, resulting in an increased alveolar dead space. What would be the effect on the partial pressure of carbon dioxide in the expired air of this patient?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Increasing dead space has the effect of decreasing the partial pressure of CO2 in the expired air. Remember that dead space is air that does not participate in gas exchange and resembles atmospheric air (PO2=150 mmHg, PCO2= 0 mmHg), so increasing dead space results in less gas exchange, and therefore a lower CO2 level in the expired air. It is important to remember that CO2 in our expired air comes from the tissues and therefore the only way to get it in the expired air is via gas exchange.

stem: What factors would decrease the diffusion capacity of a gas (ie make it harder to diffuse)?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

The diffusion capacity for any gas is equal to (area)*(diffusion coefficient for gas) ÷(thickness of the membrane). Therefore to decrease the diffusion capacity, increasing thickness or decreasing surface area would decrease the diffusion capacity, making it harder to diffuse a gas across. This is important because diseases that increase the thickness (pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary edema) or decrease surface area (emphysema) make it harder for carbon dioxide and oxygen to diffuse, which will interfere with gas exchange, decreasing the oxygen content of the blood and increasing the carbon dioxide content of the blood, both situations which will cause problems to a patient.

stem: What mechanisms can result in arterial hypoxemia (low partial pressure of oxygen in arterial blood)?
answer:
The correct answer is E.

All of the above. Decreasing PIO2 is not a common cause of arterial hypoxemia, but it can happen with increased altitude such as climbing Mount Everest, the barometric pressure decreases resulting in a lower PIO2, decreasing the PaO2. The alveolar gas equation states that PAO2= PIO2- PaCO2/0.8. Alveolar hypoventilation results in increased PaCO2, which than will decrease the PAO2, causing arterial hypoxemia if PaCO2 increases enough. Intrapulmonary shunt can cause arterial hypoxemia by allowing blood to bypass the lung and not be replenished with fresh, new air from the alveoli. This can happen in congenital heart disease, such as ventricular septal defect, where blood goes directly from the right ventricle to the left, by passing the lung. The last cause of arterial hypoxemia is ventilation/perfusion mismatch, which can be cause by lung disease. For example, if an alveolus is damaged from infection, it will have a reduced ventilation, reducing the ventilation/perfusion ratio, resulting in blood resembling venous blood (low oxygen, high carbon dioxide). Any blood that perfuses this alveolus will not get oxygen and remove carbon dioxide, therefore this can result in arterial hypoxemia if this happens in many alveoli, such as in pneumonia.

stem: Which of the following is not a mechanism for hypoxemia?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Cyanide poisoning prevents cells from taking up or utilizing oxygen from the bloodstream, and therefore the delivery of oxygen to these cells and tissues is not disturbed. Such a patient would be hypoxic, not hypoxemic. Hypoxemia refers to oxygen deficiency in the arterial blood, and may be due to reduced partial pressure of oxygen or reduced saturation of hemoglobin. This can be due to reduced rate or volume of air entering the lungs, or impaired transfer of air from the lungs to the blood. Cardiovascular causes, such as shunts, may also result in hypoxemia. Decreased FiO2 or PiO2 (fraction of inspired oxygen or inspired partial pressure of oxygen) is not often seen clinically.

stem: Carl is a 64 year old male patient who was diagnosed with COPD 3 years ago. Today, Carl visits you complaining of dyspnea. What is the most likely explanation of Carl’s dyspnea?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Dynamic hyperinflation occurs due to the ‘floppiness’ of airways in COPD patients caused by disrupted alveolar attachments, mucosal inflammation, and mucus obstruction of the lumen. Dynamic hyperinflation is a ‘trapping’ of air in the lungs, reducing inspiratory capacity and leading to a sensation of dyspnea.

stem: Which of the following is least likely to be part of a paraneoplastic syndrome?
answer:
The correct answer is E.

Paraneoplastic syndrome is a disease or symptom that results from the presence of cancer in the body, but is not due to the local presence of cancer cells. Kidney obstruction due to a tumor would not be considered a paraneoplastic syndrome, because it is due to the direct (local) effects of a tumor. All other answers are examples of possible paraneoplastic syndrome.

stem: Alex is a 14 year old male patient of yours with cystic fibrosis. Which of the following are complications that you might worry about Alex developing? (Choose 4 answers)
answer:
The correct answer is A, C, F, G.

Cystic fibrosis can cause obstruction of pancreatic ducts, leading to inflammation of eventual loss of pancreatic B-cell function. This leads to insulin insufficiency and cystic fibrosis-related diabetes. A.CORRECT Atelectasis (complete or partial collapse of the lung) is seen in cystic fibrosis due to the inherent viscosity and stickiness of the mucus, and its propensity to build up in the lungs. B. INCORRECT CF patients are prone to demineralization, retardation of bone age, and osteoporosis - bones become weaker and do not grow excessively. C. CORRECT The thick, sticky mucous of CF patients means clearing potential infectants is much more difficult. Possibility of infection should always be considered in these patients. D. INCORRECT This is not a concern specifically related to CF. E. INCORRECT This is not a concern specifically related to CF. F. CORRECT Male infertility is a common concern with CF, often due to an absence of the ductus deferens, epididymis, and seminal vesicles. (please note that female infertility/decreased fertility is also a concern due to increased viscosity of cervical mucous)

Compliance = ΔV/ΔP. In emphysema (COPD) compliance is high: the lung is easy to inflate and has low recoil. stem: A healthy man sits upright and breathes quietly from FRC. Where does most of each tidal breath go, and why?

options.html: Apices, whose alveoli are held most open
Evenly to every region of the lung
Apices, where pleural pressure is most negative
Bases, which lie on the steep part of the P-V curve
Hilar regions, closest to the large airways and bronchi

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Pleural pressure is more negative at the apex, so apical alveoli are already distended at FRC and sit on the flat, less compliant part of the pressure-volume curve. Basal alveoli are relatively compressed, sit on the steep part, and so are more compliant and receive most of the tidal volume in quiet breathing. (After a forced expiration to RV the order reverses: the first air goes to the apices.)

stem: In a healthy person at rest, which sensor provides the main minute-to-minute drive to breathe?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

The primary controller is CO2, via the central chemoreceptors in the medulla, which sense CSF pH as a reflection of PaCO2 and give minute-to-minute control. The peripheral (carotid body) chemoreceptors respond mainly to PaO2 and only become steeply active once PaO2 falls (or in chronic hypercarbia, as in COPD, where drive shifts toward them).

answer:
The correct answer is E.

He meets all three Anthonisen (Winnipeg) criteria: increased dyspnea, increased sputum volume and increased sputum purulence. With all three, antibiotic therapy is warranted because a bacterial infection is likely. Exacerbation treatment is otherwise short-acting bronchodilators and a systemic corticosteroid.
